items.title: Finite alphabets, encoded inputs, and algorithms
Recursive and recursively enumerable languages
Recursive presentations and finite presentations of groups
The trivial words of a recursively presented group form a recursively enumerable language
items.strategy: Use the normal-closure description of relators as finite products of conjugates and enumerate those products systematically.

items.title: The word problem for a fixed finite presentation
The uniform word problem for finite presentations
Solvability of the word problem does not depend on the chosen finite generating set
items.strategy: Translate words across two finite presentations of the same group and use Tietze equivalence to transport a decision procedure in either direction.

items.title: The word problem for a finitely generated free group is solvable by free reduction
items.strategy: Reduce the input word freely and use the published normal-form theorem to identify the trivial element with the empty reduced word.

items.title: Finitely generated abelian groups admit invariant-factor normal form
items.strategy: Record the exact invariant-factor classification needed for coordinate reduction; the later PID-module page proves the stronger structural theorem, but this page only cites the resulting normal form.

items.title: The word problem for finitely generated abelian groups is solvable
items.strategy: Use the cited invariant-factor normal form to write the group as Z^r plus finite torsion and decide equality by reducing the finite coordinate list modulo the invariant factors.

items.title: Free products and suitable amalgamated free products have solvable word problem
items.strategy: Run the published amalgam normal-form reduction and use the assumed factor word-problem and amalgam-membership procedures to decide each reduction step.

items.title: The conjugacy problem for a finitely generated group
The isomorphism problem for a class of finite presentations
A Markov property of finitely presented groups
Novikov-Boone: some finitely presented group has unsolvable word problem
items.strategy: Record the exact undecidability theorem as a cited scope boundary; no local proof of the Novikov-Boone construction is attempted here.

items.title: Adian-Rabin: every Markov property is undecidable on finite presentations
items.strategy: Record the exact Adian-Rabin theorem with its witness-group hypotheses visible; no local proof of the reduction is attempted on this page.

items.title: Triviality and finiteness are undecidable for finite presentations
items.strategy: Record the exact Adian-Rabin corollaries for the specific Markov properties of being trivial and being finite.

items.title: The isomorphism problem for finitely presented groups is undecidable
items.strategy: Record the classical undecidability theorem exactly as a cited scope boundary and keep it non-load-bearing on the page.

items.title: There exist finitely presented groups with unsolvable conjugacy problem
items.strategy: Record Miller's exact existence theorem as a source-backed boundary result only.

items.title: Algebraic relator area and the Dehn function of a finite presentation
Every null word has a minimal algebraic relator area
items.strategy: Use the existence of at least one relator expression and well-ordering of the natural numbers.

items.title: A recursive Dehn function yields a solution to the word problem
items.strategy: Bound the relator area of a null word by the recursive Dehn function and exhaust the finitely many relator expressions up to that bound, using free-group reduction to test equality in the ambient free group.

items.title: FALSE: every finitely presented group has solvable word problem
items.strategy: Refute with the Novikov-Boone existence theorem.

items.title: FALSE: recursively enumerable trivial words already give a decision algorithm
items.strategy: Refute by distinguishing enumeration of true instances from a halting procedure on both trivial and nontrivial words.

items.title: FALSE: an unsolvable word problem means no individual word can be decided
items.strategy: Refute by separating failure of one uniform algorithm from ad hoc proofs about particular words.

items.title: FALSE: the Novikov-Boone theorem proves only the uniform problem is unsolvable
items.strategy: Refute because the theorem already produces one fixed finitely presented group with unsolvable word problem.

items.title: FALSE: Tietze-equivalent finite presentations can differ on whether their word problem is solvable
items.strategy: Refute by transporting a decision procedure across Tietze-equivalent presentations of the same group.

title: Decision Problems for Finitely Presented Groups — Examples

items.title: Free reduction decides a word in a free group
items.strategy: Reduce an explicit word in a free basis and compare the result with the empty reduced word.

items.title: The word problem in a finite cyclic presentation
items.strategy: Write the presented group as Z modulo n and reduce the input exponent modulo n.

items.title: Conjugacy in a free group by cyclic reduction
items.strategy: Cyclically reduce two explicit words and compare their cyclic permutations using the published free-group conjugacy criterion.

items.title: Todd-Coxeter as a partial coset-enumeration procedure
items.strategy: Run a short finite coset table long enough to show how the procedure can terminate successfully without being a general decision algorithm.

items.title: Computing an algebraic relator area
items.strategy: Express a null word as a short product of conjugates of relators and show that no shorter expression exists.

items.title: Enumerating relator consequences does not decide nontriviality
items.strategy: Use a nontrivial word whose failure to appear in the positive enumeration shows why semi-decision is weaker than decision.

title: Graphs of Groups and Bass Serre Theory

items.title: A graph of groups
A maximal subtree of a connected graph
The path group of a graph of groups
The fundamental group of a graph of groups relative to a maximal tree
Different maximal trees give isomorphic graph-of-groups fundamental groups
items.strategy: Choose connecting paths between the two tree gauges and conjugate each stable edge generator across those paths to build mutually inverse homomorphisms.

items.title: Reduced words in a graph of groups
Normal form for the fundamental group of a graph of groups
items.strategy: Peel the graph off one geometric edge at a time, reducing to the published amalgam and HNN normal forms at each step.

items.title: Vertex groups embed in the fundamental group of a graph of groups
items.strategy: A nontrivial element of a vertex group is already a reduced graph-of-groups word of length zero, so normal-form uniqueness forbids collapse.

items.title: The Bass-Serre tree of a graph of groups
The Bass-Serre coset graph is a tree
items.strategy: Connectedness comes from reading reduced words as coset paths, and a reduced closed path would contradict graph-of-groups normal form.

items.title: The fundamental group acts without inversions on its Bass-Serre tree
items.strategy: Left multiplication on cosets preserves the incidence maps, and the normal form identifies the quotient graph and the vertex and edge stabilizers up to conjugacy.

items.title: The quotient graph of groups attached to a tree action
The boundary monomorphisms from stabilizers are well-defined
items.strategy: Change of orbit representatives alters the chosen attaching element by conjugation, so the resulting edge-to-vertex maps differ only by the expected inner automorphism.

items.title: Bass-Serre structure theorem
items.strategy: Choose orbit representatives and connecting lifts, map each stabilizer and non-tree edge generator into the acting group, and compare the resulting action with the Bass-Serre tree of the reconstructed graph of groups.

items.title: A one-segment graph of groups gives an amalgamated free product
items.strategy: In the one-edge case, unwind the graph-of-groups presentation and compare it directly with the published amalgam pushout description.

items.title: A one-loop graph of groups gives an HNN extension
items.strategy: Collapse the chosen maximal tree and identify the lone non-tree edge generator with the stable letter of the published HNN presentation.

items.title: A group acting freely without inversions on a tree is free
items.strategy: All stabilizers in the quotient graph of groups are trivial, so the structure theorem identifies the group with the fundamental group of a graph built only from non-tree edge generators.

items.title: The fundamental group of a graph with trivial groups is free
items.strategy: Apply the Bass-Serre action to the trivial-group graph of groups; the action is free, so the previous corollary identifies the fundamental group as free.

items.title: Kurosh subgroup theorem
items.strategy: Restrict the Bass-Serre tree action of a free product to the subgroup, read off the quotient graph of groups, and use trivial edge groups to obtain the free-product decomposition with double-coset indexing.

items.title: Grushko decomposition and rank additivity
items.strategy: Use free splittings with trivial edge groups, derive terminal freely indecomposable factors from maximality, and use Kurosh on two decompositions to compare factor conjugacy classes and the free rank.

items.title: Stallings's theorem on ends and splittings
items.strategy: Record the exact finitely generated theorem only; the ends machinery it needs lies outside this page.

items.title: FALSE: the fundamental group of a graph of groups is a topological fundamental group by definition
items.strategy: Refute because the algebraic graph-of-groups presentation is defined first and only later compared with tree actions.

items.title: FALSE: vertex stabilizers are literally the chosen vertex groups without conjugacy ambiguity
items.strategy: Refute by changing the chosen lift of a quotient vertex, which conjugates the stabilizer inside the acting group.

items.title: FALSE: every tree action is free
items.strategy: Refute with actions having nontrivial vertex stabilizers, such as the Bass-Serre action of a nontrivial amalgam.

items.title: FALSE: the quotient graph determines the acting group without stabilizer data
items.strategy: Refute by comparing nonisomorphic graphs of groups carried by the same underlying quotient graph.

items.title: FALSE: Kurosh says every subgroup of a free product is free
items.strategy: Refute because Kurosh retains conjugates of intersections with factor groups as genuine free-product factors.

title: Graphs of Groups and Bass Serre Theory — Examples

items.title: The Bass-Serre tree of a free product
items.strategy: Take a graph of groups with two vertices and trivial edge group and read the vertices and edges as cosets of the two factors.

items.title: The Bass-Serre tree of an amalgamated free product
items.strategy: Start from the one-segment graph of groups and write down the two vertex-orbit types and the common edge stabilizer.

items.title: The Bass-Serre tree of a Baumslag-Solitar group
items.strategy: Use the one-loop graph of groups description and identify the stable-letter action on the resulting tree of cosets.

items.title: A free action and the quotient-graph basis
items.strategy: Quotient a free action on a tree by a chosen maximal subtree and read the free basis from the non-tree edges.

items.title: A Kurosh decomposition of a subgroup of a free product
items.strategy: Restrict the Bass-Serre action to an explicit subgroup and read off the resulting factor intersections and free part from the quotient tree.

items.title: A graph of finite groups giving a virtually free group
items.strategy: Use finite vertex and edge stabilizers in the Bass-Serre tree and a finite quotient graph to exhibit a virtually free fundamental group.

items.title: The underlying quotient graph does not determine the acting group
items.strategy: Put different vertex or edge groups on the same underlying quotient graph and compare the resulting fundamental groups.
